items.title: A microprotein atlas of the human frontal cortex in Alzheimer’s disease
items.author: Alan Saghatelian
items.content: A new atlas identifies 1,067 unannotated microproteins in the human frontal cortex with strong spectral grades. A subset is differentially expressed in Alzheimer’s disease independently of their canonical genes, including an MKKS-derived microprotein required for normal microglial mitochondrial respiration.

items.title: Large-scale mapping of microproteins in the aged human brain
items.content: Microproteins, small proteins of 100–150 amino acids, are largely absent from reference proteomes and have been overlooked in brain and aging research. An atlas of the aged human brain catalogs over 1,000 high-confidence microproteins, including one encoded by the MKKS gene that is reduced in Alzheimer’s disease and regulates energy production in microglia.

items.title: Fibronectin mediates APOE4-driven blood–brain barrier dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease
items.author: Caghan Kizil
items.content: Bhattarai, Yilmaz and colleagues identify astrocyte-derived fibronectin as a key driver of blood–brain barrier dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease, linking APOE ε4 and amyloid pathology to vascular damage and highlighting FN1 as a potential therapeutic target.

items.title: Aging rises, yet the double burden of illness remains
items.author: Joseph L. Dieleman
items.content: Ashwin and colleagues propose a statistical framing of the epidemiological transition that categorizes global diseases into four life-stages, identifying aging-related diseases as the dominant category. As aging-related diseases tend to cluster and span many years, health systems must pivot from treating disease to preserving health through investments in all life stages.

items.title: A consensus roadmap from the SENESCENCE2030 network towards precision senescence medicine
items.author: Marco Demaria
items.content: At the SENESCENCE2030 Annual Conference and Industry–Academia Workshop held in Coimbra, Portugal, in May 2026, researchers, clinicians, industry representatives and policy stakeholders identified the major priorities required to translate recent advances in cellular senescence research into clinical practice. The resulting roadmap emphasizes the need to establish functional classifications of senescent states, develop standardized and clinically actionable biomarkers, advance precision senescence medicine, strengthen translational and regulatory frameworks, and promote international collaboration.
